questions.text: Under the checked DOE energy-design family, what should a large building metering strategy make visible?

options.text: Electrical quantities such as voltage, current, power factor, maximum demand, and energy use, with major feeder groups separated where required.
Only the monthly utility bill total, with no feeder-level separation.
Only decorative lighting loads because HVAC loads are outside energy monitoring.
Only tenant complaints, because measured electrical data is not part of energy design.

questions.rationale: The DOE guideline requires metering for major electrical quantities and calls for feeder-level grouping for lighting, chillers, AHUs, unitary equipment, and motor loads.
questions.code_citation: LEA-UTIL-007-02.mdx (Practical Application case study, lines 165–183; Analytics and Anomaly Detection, lines 69–79; End-Use Category baselines, lines 36–38)

questions.text: Which RA 11285 classification statement is source-safe for a designated establishment using annual electricity consumption?

options.text: Type 1 covers 500,000 to 4,000,000 kWh, while Type 2 covers more than 4,000,000 kWh.
Type 1 begins only above 4,000,000 kWh and Type 2 is lower.
The type is based only on the building height, not energy use.
All buildings are classified without regard to consumption thresholds.

questions.rationale: The checked RA 11285 family states the Type 1 and Type 2 designated-establishment thresholds by annual energy consumption.

questions.text: What is the safest LEA use of metering data under the checked DOE and RA 11285 families?

options.text: Use measured end-use data to support energy audits, ECCR, records, and operational decisions.
Use metering only for marketing dashboards and ignore audit records.
Replace the CECO or CEM role with a vendor dashboard.
Treat smart meters as a substitute for code-compliant electrical working space.

questions.rationale: RA 11285 covers audits, ECCR, records, and CECO/CEM responsibilities; DOE guidance supports metering and end-use grouping as a design and operations tool.
questions.code_citation: LEA-UTIL-007-02.mdx (Net Metering and Bidirectional Flow, lines 22–25; references ERC Order 2024-021)

questions.text: When locating metering and service equipment, which checked PEC idea remains important?

options.text: Provide required electrical working space, headroom, illumination, and coordination clearances.
Use the smallest closet available if the meter can still be read.
Let foreign ducts and pipes occupy the dedicated electrical space by default.
Rely on analytics software to waive physical access requirements.

questions.rationale: The PEC family includes working-space, headroom, illumination, access, and dedicated-space coordination provisions for electrical equipment.
